content:
samir: Heads-up: support reported a customer hit a hard rate-limit even though console showed low confirmed usage. They were doing long-lived streaming + toolcall chains with intermittent reconnects (acct: acct-omega). Anyone seen quota enforcement behave unexpectedly with provisional credits?

anya: Yep, saw a few similar tickets. TL;DR: quota enforcement uses confirmed ledger values, but the routing stack applies provisional local throttles based on observed streaming chunks to protect saturation. If the provisional counters are high and then later reconciled down (missing finalize), customers end up blocked during the provisional peak and then we 'refund' later, which is confusing.

lee: Can you share a representative trace?

samir: Pasted abbreviated sequence from proxy/router:
```
[router] session=sessX event=chunk tokens=1200 provisional_id=pX
[router] session=sessX event=toolcall start id=tA
[router] session=sessX event=toolcall truncated id=tA reason=upstream_disconnect
[router] session=sessX event=reconnect
[router] session=sessX event=chunk tokens=800 provisional_id=pY
[ledger_ingest] got: confirm for pY -> not present
# finalize missing for pX, pY reconciled later to lower number
```
In this case the router had incremented an in-memory provisional quota and refused new long-polling requests for ~30s, causing the app to return 429s. Later the ledger reconciliation reduced the confirmed tally and console adjusted usage down, but the customer already experienced errors.

kai: This is the classic provisional vs confirmed tension. We purposely put provisional throttles in the runtime to protect tail latencies, but the UX for customers is bad if provisional is used aggressively. Two problems: (1) provisional counters are optimistic and may never settle high enough, (2) reconciliation delta timing is variable.

anya: Proposed options: 
- Option A (conservative): Stop using provisional counters for hard quota enforcement; only use them for soft throttles (rate-slowing) and always fall back to confirmed ledger for killing requests. Less protection for spikes but fewer false 429s.
- Option B (accurate+complex): Make provisional counters authoritative for a short, configurable window (e.g., 10s) and atomically reserve provisional tokens in the ledger with TTL. If finalize reduces usage, refund the reservation. This requires fast TTL eviction and a cheap reservation path in ledger (small writes).

lee: Implementation notes for Option B: we need an idempotent reservation API: ledger.reserve(session_id, reserved_tokens, ttl, reservation_id). Reservation writes must be cheap and compact. On finalize we call ledger.confirm(session_id, final_tokens, reservation_id) which reconciles. If confirm < reserved -> ledger credits workspace. Need to be careful about races where reservations from two routers overlap (dedupe by reservation_id).

kai: Option A is simpler and lower ops cost. Our current incidents mostly stem from provisional hard enforcement on canary clusters. Maybe toggle behavior by workspace: opt-in to provisional hard-quotas for high-SLA customers that need low-latency rejection semantics.

samir: UX ideas: console should show three columns for usage windows: provisional_reserved, provisional_seen (local), confirmed_final. Add a timeline sparkline that shows provisional vs confirmed divergence so support can see when provisional enforcement triggered. And add a workspace toggle "allow provisional hard quota" with a clear tooltip explaining risk.

anya: Telemetry: emit metrics: provisional_reservations_per_min, reservation_confirm_ratio (confirm/reserve), reservation_refund_count, reservation_conflict_count. Also a histogram of reconciliation_delay (time between reservation and confirm/finalize) so we can set sensible TTLs.

lee: For rollout: start with Option A for all customers (disable hard provisional enforcement). Then run Option B as an opt-in on 2% of traffic for a week and measure: (a) number of 429s avoided, (b) extra ledger writes, (c) percentage of reservations that needed refunds and average refund size.

ops-bot: ops-bot: created canary job canary-reserve-1pct scheduled at 02:00 UTC. Logs will be pushed to #eng-platform-canary.

kai: One more gotcha: toolcalls that are retried by clients can duplicate provisional reservations if client replays and session_id changes. We need idempotency keys derived from client-side request id when available, otherwise dedupe heuristics in ledger (time-windowed).

anya: I'll draft a short RFC describing reservation API + console changes and include mockups for the toggle and timeline. Samir can own the canary run. Lee, can you add the telemetry counters to the router and ledger ingest?

lee: Yep, adding metrics. I'll also add an alert: reservation_confirm_ratio < 75% for 5m -> page oncall. That should catch weird spikes where finalize disappears.

samir: Filing ISSUE-2099 and assigning tasks. Thanks all, will post RFC link here once ready.

ops-bot: ops-bot: ISSUE-2099 created: "provisional-reservation-ledger-and-console-ux" assigned to samir, anya, lee.
